item.title: Nucleation you can poke
item.description:
On this site’s home page, the lattice spells one word after another, and every change of word briefly heats the lattice. Without that pulse the old word does not go away. The field under it has reversed, so it is no longer the equilibrium state, but at low temperature it is metastable: nothing local can undo it, because every small change costs more than it gains. Getting out of a metastable state takes a rare, collective event, which is nucleation.

The critical droplet

Start with every spin pointing down in a field that favors up. Flipping a roughly circular droplet of radius gains per spin in the bulk but pays a surface tension along its edge. In the continuum approximation of classical nucleation theory,

The surface term wins for small droplets and the bulk term for large ones, so has a maximum at the critical radius

Droplets smaller than tend to shrink and larger ones tend to grow. For the square-lattice Ising model the surface tension along a lattice axis is known exactly from Onsager’s solution: , which falls to zero at . The widget below uses that value to estimate . It is only a guide: real droplets on a lattice are not circles, and the surface tension depends on the direction of the interface.

Things to try

  • Plant droplets on either side of . At the default and the estimate is 4.3 cells, and the lattice agrees surprisingly well: in my runs, droplets of radius 4 or less melted back and droplets of radius 5 or more grew. Watch a growing droplet and it turns into a rounded square, the lattice anisotropy that the circular estimate ignores.
  • Just wait. At , the barrier is about , so spontaneous nucleation essentially never happens on this lattice. Raise or and the barrier drops quickly; at , somewhere between and , droplets start appearing on their own within seconds.
  • Sweep the field. The magnetization lags behind the field and traces a hysteresis loop, switching only once the field is strong enough for nucleation to happen on the timescale of the sweep. The loop is not a property of the material alone: it depends on how fast the field moves compared to how long nucleation takes.
  • Heat toward . The surface tension vanishes, collapses, and the loop closes.

Classical nucleation theory, with a critical nucleus set by the competition between surface and bulk free energy, is also the usual starting point for real clusters. That includes the ligand-mediated nanocluster growth in two of my papers (2019, 2020). This lattice is about the simplest system where you can watch the same idea play out spin by spin.

Further reading

  • L. Onsager, Crystal statistics. I. A two-dimensional model with an order–disorder transition, Phys. Rev. 65, 117–149 (1944).
  • P. A. Rikvold, H. Tomita, S. Miyashita, and S. W. Sides, Metastable lifetimes in a kinetic Ising model: Dependence on field and system size, Phys. Rev. E 49, 5080–5090 (1994).

item.title: The 404 page is doing Bayesian inference
item.description:
The spins on this site’s 404 page and home page are a biased Ising model. An external field shaped like the text pushes spins up inside the glyphs and down outside them, and the lattice is cooled until the pattern condenses out of thermal noise. The same equations, read differently, are one of the classic methods for restoring noisy images.

Prior, likelihood, posterior

Take a binary picture , one value per pixel. A reasonable prior belief about pictures is that neighboring pixels tend to agree, which is exactly what an Ising model says:

Now observe the picture through a noisy channel that flips each pixel independently with probability . For one pixel, is if and otherwise, which can be written as

Bayes’ rule multiplies the two:

That is a biased Ising model at . The coupling is the prior, and the external field is the data: each observed pixel pulls its spin toward what was seen, with a strength set by how much the channel can be trusted.

Gibbs sampling a picture of Gibbs

To draw samples from this posterior, visit each pixel in turn and set it from its conditional distribution given its neighbors,

Physicists call this heat-bath dynamics. Geman and Geman, who introduced this approach to image restoration in 1984, called it the Gibbs sampler, after the Gibbs distribution it samples. So the default picture below is Gibbs himself.

The hidden picture is binarized (for the portraits, with a little edge enhancement so they read as pen sketches rather than silhouettes), flipped at random to make the observation, and then sampled from the posterior. The last panel averages the samples; its sign at each pixel is the estimate that minimizes the expected number of wrong pixels.

Things to try

  • Set . The prior disappears and every pixel is on its own. The posterior mean just agrees with the observation, so the error equals the flip probability.
  • Raise slowly. Neighbors start voting, isolated flips get outvoted, and the error drops well below .
  • Keep going past . That is , the critical coupling of the two-dimensional Ising model, beyond which the prior on its own would order the whole lattice. The best reconstructions sit just above it, around . Push further and the prior starts erasing real detail (eyes, glasses, beard texture, the water around the helix) and the error climbs again.
  • Push toward 0.5. The field goes to zero, the data stop carrying information, and the posterior relaxes back to the prior.

The trade-off in the third item has a physical reading I ran into while tuning the lattice on the 404 page. A feature survives only if the field energy it gains outweighs the domain-wall energy it costs: a stroke has to be wider than about pixels, and a hole enclosed by a stroke needs an area-to-perimeter ratio above about . In the statistical reading, the same inequality says how much evidence a small feature needs before the prior stops smoothing it away. That is a bias–variance trade-off in a physicist’s vocabulary.

The same question, of how much structure to assume and what it costs you, comes up whenever physics is recovered from noisy data, as in denoising single-atom potentials.

Further reading

  • S. Geman and D. Geman, Stochastic relaxation, Gibbs distributions, and the Bayesian restoration of images, IEEE Trans. Pattern Anal. Mach. Intell. 6, 721–741 (1984).
  • J. Besag, On the statistical analysis of dirty pictures, J. R. Stat. Soc. B 48, 259–279 (1986). Introduces iterated conditional modes, a fast deterministic alternative to sampling.
  • D. M. Greig, B. T. Porteous, and A. H. Seheult, Exact maximum a posteriori estimation for binary images, J. R. Stat. Soc. B 51, 271–279 (1989). Shows the most probable image can be found exactly with a minimum cut.

Portraits of J. Willard Gibbs (before 1903) and Ludwig Boltzmann (1902) are in the public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. The helix frame is from the replica-exchange simulations described on the helix–coil project page.

item.title: A place for working notes
item.description:
Research papers are necessarily compressed. The false starts, implementation details, useful references, and small conceptual connections that make the work possible rarely survive into the final manuscript.

This section is a place for those pieces: notes on computational chemistry and statistical physics, practical details from scientific software, and short explanations of ideas I want to understand more clearly.

The aim is simple—write things down while they are still useful, and make them clear enough that someone else can build on them.
